content:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Cost visibility + Optimize ROI review (Arcadia)
Date: 2026-02-13
Time: 4:00pm - 4:52pm PT
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Aditya Rao, Hassan Mirza, Arjun Desai, Felix Schneider, Chloe Martin
- Arcadia LegalTech: Sarah Kim (Director of Data Platform), Miguel Alvarez (Staff ML Engineer), Priya Patel (Finance Ops)

Summary (auto-generated)
- Arcadia asked for a clear explanation of how Redwood computes request cost and savings estimates for batching, caching, and quantization.
- Redwood walked through the cost breakdown taxonomy (prefill vs decode, cache hits/misses, batch efficiency, and overhead allocation) and clarified which components are estimations vs metered.
- Arcadia highlighted concerns about “optimistic” what-if results when cache warm-rate is assumed too high and requested transparency on assumptions and confidence.
- Redwood agreed to provide a taxonomy 1-pager and to run a backtest using Arcadia workload summaries to calibrate what-if recommendations.

Topics
- Console cost breakdown semantics: prefill vs decode, KV cache, batching/queueing, and overhead
- Optimize what-if projections: batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization profile changes
- Assumptions: cache warm-rate, request mix stability, batch formation and tail latency constraints
- Confidence intervals / uncertainty and “quality guardrails” for quantization
- Reconciling Console views with invoice / finance reporting windows

Questions (from customer)
- What exactly is included in “overhead” and can we see it separately from request-attributable cost?
- For caching savings: do you assume the cache is warm? How do you model warm-up and churn?
- For batching savings: are you assuming we can tolerate higher queue time? Is tail latency constraint part of the model?
- For quantization: do you factor accuracy/quality degradation or is it purely throughput/cost?
- Why might Console numbers differ from invoice totals today, and what changes once you standardize the cost model?

Action items
- Redwood to share a short taxonomy + field semantics doc, plus guardrails on what-if parameters.
- Arcadia to share a one-week workload summary for backtesting.

---

Transcript

[00:00] Aditya Rao: Alright, we should be recording. Thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is to go a layer deeper than the usual demo. You all had questions on, like, how the sausage is made on cost breakdown and then the Optimize ROI numbers.

[00:14] Sarah Kim: Yeah. We like the UI, but we need to be able to defend it internally. The big thing is, finance will ask “what is included in savings” and “why does it not match our cloud spend,” like those kinds of questions.

[00:28] Priya Patel: Exactly. I don’t need perfect, but I need consistent definitions. If you say we save 23%, I need to know 23% of what.

[00:37] Felix Schneider: Totally. That’s actually why we wanted Chloe on as well. Console and Optimize are consuming the same cost primitives going forward. Today it can look a little… not mismatched, but the definitions aren’t always obvious.

[00:52] Chloe Martin: Yeah, and we can talk about what’s changing in the next few weeks as we standardize the cost model.

[00:58] Miguel Alvarez: I’ll be the annoying one on the technical side. When we did the Optimize trial, the caching what-if basically said “enable cache, save 40%.” We turned on a cache in our own stack before, and it was… not 40. It’s more like 10 to 15 and it depends on churn.

[01:17] Hassan Mirza: That’s fair. The biggest lever in that projection is the warm-rate / reuse assumption. If the model assumes a high hit rate or a stable prefix distribution, it will overstate.

[01:28] Aditya Rao: Maybe we start with the breakdown taxonomy, then go into each what-if lever and the assumptions behind it.

[01:35] Sarah Kim: Works.

[01:37] Aditya Rao: Felix, do you want to share the breakdown definitions at a high level?

[01:41] Felix Schneider: Sure. So, at the request level, we decompose “request-attributable” cost into stages. The big split is prefill vs decode. Prefill is ingesting the prompt / context, decode is generating tokens.

[01:55] Miguel Alvarez: Prefill is basically attention on the entire input, right.

[01:58] Felix Schneider: Yeah, and decode is step-by-step generation. Then within that, we have adjustments for caching and batching. When KV cache hits, you’re effectively skipping compute for the reused prefix. So we’ll show a “cache savings” or “cached tokens” component.

[02:15] Priya Patel: And overhead?

[02:17] Felix Schneider: Overhead is where it gets sticky. Overhead is cost not directly attributable to a single request’s token compute. Things like idle capacity, control plane overhead, maybe some baseline reserved GPU cost depending on deployment mode.

[02:34] Chloe Martin: The key is we separate it in the breakdown. You’ll see request compute vs overhead allocation. And the allocation policy is explicit, meaning we’re not hiding it inside “per token.”

[02:45] Sarah Kim: So if I’m on Dedicated, overhead can be large if I’m underutilizing.

[02:50] Chloe Martin: Exactly. And that’s why you want to see it separately.

[02:54] Miguel Alvarez: But in Hosted, overhead is pooled across customers.

[02:58] Aditya Rao: Right, Hosted is more like blended pricing and pooled utilization, so the request attribution is more stable. Dedicated and Private are where overhead and utilization are very visible.

[03:12] Priya Patel: Okay. But when Optimize says “savings,” does it include overhead or not?

[03:18] Hassan Mirza: Great question. Today, most of the what-if levers are framed as savings on request-attributable compute. But for Dedicated, we also compute an “effective savings” that can include overhead, if the recommendation changes utilization.

[03:34] Priya Patel: That’s… subtle.

[03:36] Hassan Mirza: Yeah. If you’re paying for reserved capacity and you’re idle, then reducing per-request compute doesn’t immediately change your bill, unless it allows you to downsize capacity or absorb more traffic. So we need to be careful in how we label it.

[03:52] Aditya Rao: This is one of the doc clarifications coming out of these calls: we’ll label “unit cost savings” vs “spend savings,” and spend savings requires a capacity change or increased load.

[04:04] Sarah Kim: Good. Because our CFO will ask why a “savings” didn’t show up.

[04:10] Felix Schneider: And to Miguel’s earlier point: cache savings projections also depend on hit rate. If we’re using defaults, it can be optimistic.

[04:18] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, like, we have a long-tail set of legal doc prompts. It’s not like a call center script.

[04:26] Hassan Mirza: Exactly. So for caching, our model uses three inputs ideally: (1) observed prefix reuse distribution, (2) cache retention / TTL, and (3) warm-rate, i.e. what fraction of traffic arrives after the relevant prefixes are in cache.

[04:43] Sarah Kim: Do you actually measure warm-rate or is it inferred?

[04:46] Hassan Mirza: Inferred or user-provided today. We can infer reuse in logs, but warm-rate depends on cache size and churn and time locality.

[04:56] Miguel Alvarez: So if you don’t know, you assume, like, 80%?

[04:59] Hassan Mirza: Historically some prototypes assumed a high default. We’re changing that. The current recommendation engine is moving toward conservative defaults and showing a range.

[05:11] Aditya Rao: Yeah, like “best case / expected / worst case” instead of a single number.

[05:17] Priya Patel: Please. A range is easier to present than a magic number.

[05:22] Arjun Desai: For quantization it’s similar. The ROI depends on throughput delta and any constraints from quality. We can measure throughput improvements fairly well. Quality is the hard part.

[05:34] Miguel Alvarez: So do you incorporate quality? Like eval scores?

[05:37] Arjun Desai: We incorporate guardrails. Think of it as: we only recommend quantization profiles that are “allowed” for that model and that workload class. But the cost model itself is not a quality model. It will expose “assumptions” and “confidence.”

[05:55] Sarah Kim: When you say “allowed,” based on what.

[05:58] Arjun Desai: A combination of our internal eval harness results and any customer-provided prompt sets if you connect them. But for v1, it’s mostly our side.

[06:09] Felix Schneider: And in the breakdown, quantization appears as a profile identifier and then a cost multiplier / throughput multiplier, not “we promise quality is unchanged.”

[06:18] Miguel Alvarez: Got it. So I should not take it as “this is free.”

[06:22] Arjun Desai: Exactly.

[06:25] Aditya Rao: Let’s hit batching, because that’s the other big lever.

[06:29] Sarah Kim: Yeah, especially because we have strict latency for interactive.

[06:33] Hassan Mirza: Batching savings come from higher GPU utilization. The model looks at: concurrency, request arrival process, max batch size, and the scheduler. It also accounts for queue time.

[06:48] Miguel Alvarez: Does it constrain p95 latency? Or is it just “batch bigger.”

[06:53] Hassan Mirza: We include a latency budget, but it’s only as good as the input. If you say “I can tolerate +20ms queue,” we’ll batch more. If you say “no queueing,” savings is smaller.

[07:07] Sarah Kim: In the UI today, I don’t remember seeing that knob.

[07:10] Aditya Rao: You’re right. In the UI it’s simplified. Under the hood, the what-if API has bounds and we’re considering surfacing it as a “latency sensitivity” selection.

[07:23] Chloe Martin: Also, for Console, we report observed batch sizes and observed queue times. That can calibrate what-if.

[07:30] Priya Patel: I’m going to ask the invoice question. We got a small mismatch in another vendor where their “console cost” didn’t match billing. How do you avoid that.

[07:41] Chloe Martin: Currently we have multiple definitions in different places. We’re actively standardizing it. The new system is a single cost model spec and API. Console and Optimize both call it, and the billing hooks will consume the same primitives.

[07:57] Priya Patel: So the invoice is still separate system but uses same inputs.

[08:01] Chloe Martin: Exactly. The invoice has taxes, credits, contract stuff, but the metering primitives like token counts, cache hits, batch efficiency, those will be the same.

[08:14] Sarah Kim: Can you say what’s in overhead, like concretely.

[08:18] Felix Schneider: Concretely: in Hosted, we attribute request compute and then the “overhead” is mostly a blended allocation of platform costs, plus the fact that not every GPU is 100% utilized every second. In Dedicated, overhead includes idle time on your reserved pool.

[08:36] Miguel Alvarez: Idle time is not overhead, it’s the bill.

[08:39] Felix Schneider: Totally, and that’s why we separate “compute” vs “utilization/idle.” It’s the same dollars, but different levers.

[08:48] Hassan Mirza: From an optimization standpoint, batching and caching reduce compute per request; utilization improvements can reduce idle, but only if your workload is big enough or you can scale down.

[09:02] Priya Patel: So when you show “cost per 1K tokens,” is that compute-only or includes idle.

[09:08] Felix Schneider: In Hosted, it’s close to compute-only because idle is pooled. In Dedicated, we can show both: “attributed” and “effective” including overhead allocation. We need to label it better.

[09:23] Sarah Kim: Okay. That’s what we need for internal comms.

[09:27] Aditya Rao: Let’s address Miguel’s concern directly: why caching what-if looked like 40%.

[09:34] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah.

[09:36] Hassan Mirza: If the assumed hit rate is like 0.6 and the cached portion is large (say 2K tokens reused), the prefill compute drops a lot. But if your real hit rate is 0.2, it’s much smaller.

[09:52] Miguel Alvarez: In our world it might be 0.2 or less. Also it depends by tenant.

[09:58] Hassan Mirza: Multi-tenant is exactly where the warm-rate matters too. If the cache is partitioned per tenant, your effective size per tenant is smaller.

[10:07] Sarah Kim: We’d need tenant isolation.

[10:09] Aditya Rao: Then we should not assume a global shared cache. We’d model it as per-tenant cache pools. That reduces warm-rate.

[10:18] Priya Patel: So can we input that.

[10:20] Hassan Mirza: In the what-if API, yes. In the UI, not fully yet.

[10:24] Felix Schneider: And, to be transparent, we’re adding guardrails so we don’t output crazy optimistic savings without clearly listing assumptions.

[10:35] Sarah Kim: That’s good. Because if we sell this internally and it doesn’t pan out…

[10:40] Aditya Rao: Yep, understood.

[10:44] Chloe Martin: Also, we’re planning to add an “assumptions” section in the response, so it’s programmatically visible.

[10:52] Miguel Alvarez: Nice.

[11:00] Aditya Rao: Let’s talk quantization. Arjun, can you outline the cost model part.

[11:05] Arjun Desai: Sure. Quantization profiles are identified in our model catalog. Each profile has expected throughput multiplier, memory footprint changes, and sometimes constraints like “not supported for function calling” or similar. The cost model uses those multipliers to project cost per token and latency.

[11:25] Miguel Alvarez: So it’s like: if you go fp16 to int8, throughput up, cost down.

[11:29] Arjun Desai: Exactly, plus you might fit more concurrent requests, which helps batching.

[11:35] Sarah Kim: But quality.

[11:37] Arjun Desai: Quality is handled via guardrails. We won’t recommend a profile if internal evals show regression above a threshold. But it’s not zero risk. That’s why we want to attach a confidence label.

[11:55] Priya Patel: And do you show confidence today.

[11:58] Arjun Desai: Not in the UI in a strong way. It’s in progress.

[12:04] Aditya Rao: We can send you a writeup of the methodology and what v1 vs v2 will include.

[12:10] Sarah Kim: Please.

[12:13] Felix Schneider: Also, Console will show which quantization profile actually ran for requests, because otherwise you can’t reconcile.

[12:22] Miguel Alvarez: That matters. We’ve seen systems where the “desired config” is not what ran.

[12:27] Chloe Martin: Exactly. We’re tying it to runtime-exported identifiers.

[12:34] Sarah Kim: You said earlier prefill vs decode. How do you measure it? Is it just token counts.

[12:41] Felix Schneider: It’s token counts and stage-level attribution. The runtime exports “prefill tokens” and “decode tokens,” plus cache hits that effectively reduce prefill tokens billed/attributed.

[12:54] Miguel Alvarez: “Billed” meaning invoice.

[12:56] Felix Schneider: Sorry, I mean “attributed cost.” Billing can be separate but uses same primitives.

[13:02] Priya Patel: Got it.

[13:05] Sarah Kim: I’m going to ask an edge case. We do rerank and embed too.

[13:10] Aditya Rao: For embeddings, it’s simpler. It’s mostly prefill-like compute. Rerank depends on model type, but we still split stages.

[13:20] Miguel Alvarez: So for Optimize, do you recommend batching for embeddings too.

[13:24] Hassan Mirza: Yes, and batching tends to be huge for embeddings. But again, depends on latency tolerance.

[13:33] Priya Patel: So what should we do next to validate these numbers.

[13:38] Aditya Rao: I think we run a backtest. If you can share a week of summary stats—doesn’t have to be raw prompts—like distribution of input/output tokens, concurrency, and maybe an estimate of cacheability, we can compute projected savings with conservative assumptions and show a range.

[13:58] Sarah Kim: We can do that.

[14:00] Miguel Alvarez: We can do token histograms, QPS by hour. Cacheability is harder but we can approximate by “same template.”

[14:07] Hassan Mirza: Even a rough “top N prefixes reuse” is helpful.

[14:13] Sarah Kim: I’ll see what we can export.

[14:16] Priya Patel: And we need the taxonomy doc.

[14:18] Felix Schneider: Yep, we’ll send a one-pager plus a sample payload so you can see the fields.

[14:25] Chloe Martin: And I’ll add notes on how we handle degradation. If the cost model service is slow, Console might use cached results, and that can change freshness but not definitions.

[14:39] Miguel Alvarez: Wait, if it uses cached results, could it be wrong.

[14:42] Chloe Martin: It could be slightly stale, but consistent. Like last known good. We’d rather show slightly stale cost than time out.

[14:52] Sarah Kim: As long as it’s labeled.

[14:54] Chloe Martin: Yep.

[15:00] Aditya Rao: I want to circle back to the “40% savings” you saw. In addition to warm-rate, another source of optimism is assuming you can reuse across requests even when there’s personalization tokens.

[15:13] Miguel Alvarez: Yep, we have user-specific disclaimers.

[15:16] Hassan Mirza: So that reduces reuse length. That should be reflected if we compute reuse from your logs.

[15:23] Sarah Kim: In a pilot, can Optimize learn from our data.

[15:27] Aditya Rao: Yes, in a pilot we can use your telemetry to compute actual cache hit rates and then calibrate the what-if.

[15:36] Priya Patel: Is that extra cost.

[15:38] Aditya Rao: No, that’s part of the pilot. The main thing is data sharing and permissions.

[15:44] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[15:47] Felix Schneider: One more nuance: “cache hits” can mean different things. There’s prefix cache at the tokenizer level, KV cache at the runtime level, and application-level caching. We’re mainly talking KV/prefix caching in the runtime.

[16:03] Miguel Alvarez: Good to clarify. We do application caching too.

[16:07] Hassan Mirza: App caching is even better sometimes, but it changes semantics. The cost model can include it as a routing state, but v1 is focusing on runtime caching.

[16:19] Sarah Kim: So if we already do app caching, your cache ROI is lower.

[16:23] Hassan Mirza: Exactly.

[16:26] Priya Patel: This is why I need definitions. Otherwise everyone says “cache” and means something else.

[16:32] Aditya Rao: 100%.

[16:36] (cross talk)

[16:38] Sarah Kim: Can you also explain how you handle “batch efficiency.” Like, is it actual measured batch size.

[16:45] Felix Schneider: In Console, we show measured. In what-if, we simulate with constraints. Batch efficiency is a function of arrival rates and scheduler. We represent it as effective tokens per GPU-second, basically.

[17:00] Miguel Alvarez: Tokens per GPU-second is what we track too.

[17:03] Felix Schneider: Great. Then we can speak the same language.

[17:08] Aditya Rao: Maybe we pivot and talk about how Arcadia would use this day-to-day. Sarah, what view do you want.

[17:14] Sarah Kim: Two things. One is per-model cost breakdown: what’s driving cost, prefill vs decode, and how much is idle. Second is “what if we switch model or quant profile,” and I need to see a credible ROI.

[17:30] Priya Patel: And I need to reconcile monthly spend.

[17:33] Chloe Martin: For monthly spend, we’ll align reporting windows. Some drift can come from telemetry lag—like if metering data arrives late.

[17:42] Priya Patel: We’ve seen that. Like dashboards show one thing then two days later it changes.

[17:48] Chloe Martin: Exactly. We’ll label data freshness and we have drift monitoring. If drift exceeds a threshold, we alert internally.

[17:58] Miguel Alvarez: What’s drift here.

[18:00] Felix Schneider: Drift is predicted cost vs observed infra spend. It can happen due to missing metrics or misattribution.

[18:09] Sarah Kim: Like if you miscount prefill tokens.

[18:11] Felix Schneider: Yes. Or if the runtime reports cache hits wrong. We had a bug recently where prefill/decode split was off for a certain path. That’s the kind of thing drift monitoring catches.

[18:26] Sarah Kim: Makes sense.

[18:29] Aditya Rao: We’re almost at the half. Any other pointed questions.

[18:34] Miguel Alvarez: One more. When you do “what-if batching,” are you holding constant the model and hardware.

[18:41] Hassan Mirza: Yes, unless you also change deployment config. What-if payload can specify hardware SKU and region, or “use current.”

[18:50] Miguel Alvarez: Okay.

[18:52] Sarah Kim: I want to know if you account for capacity constraints. Like, if the GPU is saturated.

[18:57] Hassan Mirza: Yes, we include saturation. But again, it needs telemetry: queue depth, utilization, etc.

[19:05] Chloe Martin: That’s part of why we’re standardizing runtime inputs.

[19:10] Priya Patel: So to summarize, for now you’ll send docs and we’ll send workloads.

[19:15] Aditya Rao: Exactly.

[19:18] (short pause)

[19:20] Felix Schneider: One thing I want to make explicit: when we say “cost,” internal cost model is about unit economics, not necessarily customer price. Hosted pricing may include margin. We should be careful what we share.

[19:34] Sarah Kim: We’re fine with relative. We just need to understand the breakdown.

[19:38] Priya Patel: Yeah, don’t share your margin, just give consistent compute attribution.

[19:44] Aditya Rao: For this pilot, we’ll focus on relative improvements and consistent metrics. We can talk about commercial terms separately.

[19:52] Sarah Kim: Great.

[19:55] Hassan Mirza: Also, we’ll include in the doc a note that “savings” in Dedicated can mean “capacity freed,” not “dollars saved” unless you resize.

[20:05] Priya Patel: Yes. Please bold that.

[20:08] Aditya Rao: Noted.

[20:10] (laughter)

[20:12] Sarah Kim: Okay, can we do a quick example. Let’s say 2k input, 300 output. Where does most cost sit.

[20:20] Felix Schneider: Often prefill dominates for long inputs, decode dominates for long outputs. For 2k in and 300 out, prefill is significant. If you can cache the first 1.5k, you cut most of prefill.

[20:35] Miguel Alvarez: And that’s where the 40% comes from.

[20:38] Hassan Mirza: Exactly.

[20:41] Sarah Kim: But only if reused.

[20:43] Hassan Mirza: Right.

[20:45] Arjun Desai: And quantization impacts both, but it’s more uniform: it speeds up compute for both stages.

[20:54] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[20:56] Priya Patel: I’m good.

[20:58] Aditya Rao: Let’s do recap and next steps then.

[21:02] Aditya Rao: (recap) We’ll send: (1) taxonomy + field semantics one-pager, (2) cache warm-rate guardrails and ranges, (3) quantization methodology note, and (4) sample payload mapping to Console breakdown. You’ll send a week workload summary. Then we meet again in ~10 days.

[21:27] Sarah Kim: Works.

[21:28] Miguel Alvarez: Works.

[21:29] Priya Patel: Works.

[21:31] Aditya Rao: Great. We’ll follow up by email.

[21:35] (call continues with scheduling / calendar details)

[22:10] Sarah Kim: Next Thursday same time should work.

[22:13] Aditya Rao: I’ll have my ops send it.

[22:16] Chloe Martin: Thanks all.

[22:18] Felix Schneider: Thank you.

[22:20] (end)

Note: Transcript auto-stops early due to recording cutoff; remaining time was scheduling and calendar coordination.
